description:
Black Locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) found on Macoskey Center trails. They have alternate, odd-pinnate leaflets. This species is native to eastern and southern parts of the United States, preferring moist, well drained soils. Black Locusts prefer full sun to partial sun/shade. They are hard wood deciduous trees, with leaves which fall in autumn and white hanging flowers which bloom in the springtime - they also exhibit legume “pods.” Black Locust trees have invasive traits that enable them to spread aggressively in some areas, however no research has been declared them so pervasive they cannot be recommended for planting sites. 

Other tree species in the area include Black Walnut (Juglans nigra), Staghorn Sumac (Rhus hirta) and Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides).

All of these species grow in relatively close range and tend to prefer either full or partial sun along forest edges. The soil for the most part in this region is considered moist due to the nearby wetland regions. I would assume because of this, they depend on a lot of the same resources, nutrients, temperature range and amounts of precipitation.

description:
Black Locust Robinia pseudoacacia Is native in eastern United Stated and considered invasive species in some areas. Another common name is False Acacia and is a relative of the pea and bean. 
Black locust reaches a typical height of 40–100 feet (12–30 m). Black Locust can often grow as a weed trees, upright with a straight trunk, in sunlight and a dried soil. Young trees are often spiny, but mature trees often lack spines.
Black Locust trees bloom in early springs and have intensely fragrant flowers and produce large amounts of nectar. In Romania the flowers are sometimes used to produce a sweet and perfumed jam, honey and are also eaten as beignets after being coated in batter and fried in oil.
The wood is very hard and is used for furniture, flooring, paneling, fence posts, and small watercraft. It is highly valued as firewood for wood-burning stoves but  is not suitable for fireplaces.

description:
A black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) tree was found behind the student center in rocky soil along a road on 9/16. Their leaves were up to approximately 10inches long, made up of pinnately compounded oval leaflets (picture 1) The bark is light gray in color and deeply furrowed with ridges (6). The tree was not flowering at the time and there were no seed pods, but there were thorns on the branches which helped me to identify it (3). 

The daily high of the day was 73° F with a low of 44° F. The temperature at the time was 73° F. Wind speed was 8 mph coming from the southwest. Precipitation was at 0 inches with 57% humidity. It was mostly cloudy out. 

Nearby, there were Goldenrod (Solidago Sp.) and Staghorn Sumac (Rhus hirta (typhina)) (4). Like the black locust, these species also do well in western PA, specifically along forest edges and 
roadsides as they need at least partial sunlight to survive. Another interesting observation is that this tree was covered in ants (5). This makes me wonder if the ants are infesting the tree, and if they get nutrients from it.

The black locust is also VERY suitable as a natural pest and weather resistant building material, and is frequently used in many outdoor projects.

I went in for a visit on October 13, 2020 and took a preliminary inventory (partial not complete) of what could be observed on an initial walk-through. My observations are summarized as follows. Observers can see Emigration Creek flowing (that is actual water flowing) in several spots along the walkway and it passes underneath the walkway and then runs westward toward the Westminster College area across 1300 East. What is interesting is that Emigration Creek (further upstream) remains “dry” east (and north) within and of Wasatch Hollow Open Space and Nature Preserve. There is a natural spring in Wasatch Hollow Open Space which serves as a water source and feeds into the creek flowing west (and south). There were many kinds of trees: Cottonwoods, Siberia Elms, Locust, Southern Catalpa, and Box Elder Maples, and few Pines and Spruces along the walkway. Many of the Cottonwoods were very large and they ran along the creekside. I could hear several Fox Squirrels and saw one in a tree, but I was not able to take an image. There were also Peafowl on the grounds. I was not able to observe any others birds except for what I am sure were a few Black-capped Chickadees (able to identify by the calls). Temperature was 75 degrees. Winds from south-southwest at 8 mph.

description:
From Wikipedia:

each leaf contains many smaller leaf like structures called leaflets, which are roughly paired on either side of the stem that runs through the leaf (rachis). There is typically one leaflet at the tip of the leaf (odd pinnate), and the leaves are alternately arranged on the stem. Each leaf is 6–14 inches (15–36 cm) long and contains 9-19 leaflets, each being 1–2 inches (2.5–5.1 cm)long, and .25–.75 inches (0.64–1.91 cm) wide. The leaflets are rounded or slightly indented at the tip and typically rounded at the base. The leaves come out of the bud folded in half, yellow green, covered with silvery down which soon disappears. Each leaflet initially has a minute stipel, which quickly falls, and is connected to the (rachis) by a short stem or petiolule. The leaves are attached to the branch with slender hairy petioles which are grooved and swollen at the base. The stipules are linear, downy, membranous at first and occasionally develop into prickles. The leaves appear relatively late in spring. Thanks

description: There is a young Black Locust volunteering in the rain gardens just outside of NKU's Science Center. These are very common trees here and the pods are light and easily blown into new territory. This sapling is at the perfect stage to see the paired spines that are the most distinctive feature of these trees. Spines are leaves or parts of leaves that are modified to be sharp and protective. Here, they are modified stipules, which are structures paired at the base of most legume leaves (and other types) and that are usually soft and harmless. As the tree gets older and the branches are tougher and farther from the ground, it will make fewer and smaller spines. Spines are usually largest on young, succulent, close-to-the ground growth, where herbivores like deer might be tempted to try it. Black Locust is most often confused with Honey Locust, but that species has thorns, which are modified twigs. Black Locust also has pinnately compound leaves with leaflets over 1" long, whereas Honey Locust often has bipinnately (twice-divided) compound leaves with small, less than 1" long leaflets.

Disturbed lowland woods with a canopy of various native hardwoods, a serious invasion of Norway maple, and a typical understory composed of mostly invasive species like Privets, Burning Bush, and Multiflora Rose.

The southwest side of the loop has almost no native tree regeneration. There are some huge bitternut and shagbark hickories here, but almost every young tree growing here is a Norway maple. There are probably a couple hundred of them between 2-6" that would be great to remove at this stage. The northern section of the loop is dense with Ligustrum obtusifolium. Besides Carpinus carolinana and a few Viburnum prunifolium, a native understory is non-existent.
